items.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Never had a bass player unless Wilbur Ware came out and played.

ctx.x: But you weren’t improvising much off of those tunes in that situation.

Sometimes you get inspired. Because the ladies would come back and say, “Now you kind of lost me out there. Will you please play my music?”, which was over and over, reading it. You stuck in as much as you could. But you did learn those tunes, and you learned them correctly, by the correct chorus, because those guys out there were mostly musicians – at the time that I went out there, were mostly older guys who were just out there, because $10 a night for eight hours? After a while, you got to love those guys,…
But they did enough different tunes that you could learn a whole lot of tunes?

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Chris Anderson Henderson, Van Vaughn Freeman

ctx.x: Oh, well, Nicky Hill come up a little later. Nicky Hill and Wilbur -- I guess Wilbur was playing around -- but I was working club dates -- and oh yeah, going back to this, I worked up at a place called the Argyle Show Lounge, up on the North Side. There was a tenor player named Gypsy -- a white tenor player. He loved Pres -- he played just like him. When I met Lee Konitz -- and oh, that piano player out of Chicago -- a whole lot of white Chicago musicians; I started getting gigs over there with these guys, you…

And they'd come on the South Side jam sessions, you know, and so I started getting jobs over there -- and oh, I had all kind of little gigs -- a gig here and a gig there. Different people. Chris Anderson Henderson, Van Vaughn Freeman ... the Freeman brothers; Van Buzz Buzz and George, and a piano player named Jo Jo Parnell.
Were you playing with Chris at this time?
